keep: A proprietary box is just a box; a universal one is an economic system. Give the standard away.
title: The Box
sub: How a steel rectangle rebuilt world trade
claim: The container was not a technology problem. It was a standards and labour problem.
lede: On 26 April 1956 a converted tanker carried fifty-eight truck bodies from Newark to Houston. McLean's accountants put the cost of loading her at 15.8 cents a ton, against $5.83 for an ordinary cargo ship.
copy: Before the container, loading a ship was a craft. Gangs of longshoremen stowed barrels, sacks, crates and drums by hand, fitting irregular cargo into an irregular hold. Loading and unloading could account for more than a third of the total cost of a voyage. New York and London each had more than fifty thousand registered dockworkers in the early 1950s. The Ideal-X figures are worth memorising, and worth reading closely. McLean's own accountants estimated about 15.8 cents a ton to load her, against $5.83 a ton for an average break-bulk ship. That is one company's estimate of loading cost, for one ship. Levinson, who reports it, also warns that the freight-cost data from the mid-1950s through the 1970s "are so severely deficient that they will never provide conclusive proof."

Malcom McLean was a trucking man, not a shipping man, which is the point. He was not trying to improve ships; he was trying to stop unloading his trailers. Being an outsider let him see the whole door-to-door journey as one system, and the industry's optimisation of each leg separately as the actual problem.

The hard part was never the steel box. It was standardisation — corner castings, lengths, stacking strength, twist-lock fittings — which required competitors to agree, and the agreement took years of negotiation that nobody puts in the story. ISO's recommendations fixed dimensions in 1968 and corner fittings in 1970. The corner fitting that became the standard was Keith Tantlinger's design, patented in Sea-Land's name, and Sea-Land released it so that anyone could build to it. And it was labour: containerisation destroyed a specific, powerful, well-organised craft, and the settlements with the dockworkers' unions were a precondition for the thing working at all. The technology was ready years before the institutions were.

The payoff shows up as an entire economic geography. Once freight cost approaches zero relative to goods value, it stops making sense to manufacture near your customers and starts making sense to manufacture wherever it is cheapest and ship. Levinson's numbers on the Asian export surge — Korean exports to the United States tripling between 1969 and 1973, Taiwan's total exports tripling in three years — describe a world being replumbed. The cause is his attribution. He credits cheaper shipping, and the trade figures alone cannot separate it from everything else that moved at the same time.

timeline.t: The Ideal-X sails from Newark to Houston with 58 truck bodies on deck.
Tantlinger's patent for stackable freight containers is granted, assigned to Sea-Land Service.
Sea-Land's weekly container service across the Atlantic begins; the Fairland reaches Rotterdam on 3 May.
ISO recommendations fix dimensions (1968) and corner fittings (1970), so any box fits any ship and any crane.
Korean exports to the United States treble; Taiwan's total exports treble in three years.

contested: Whether the container drove globalisation is argued with numbers on both sides. Bernhofen, El-Sahli and Kneller (Journal of International Economics, 2016) offered what they call the first identification strategy for the question and found "economically large concurrent and cumulative effects", supporting the container as a driver of twentieth-century globalisation. The strongest objection is David Hummels (Journal of Economic Perspectives, 2007): "The ad-valorem impact of ocean shipping costs is not much lower today than in the 1950s, with technological advances largely trumped by adverse cost shocks." Air freight, by his measure, fell by an order of magnitude. The two do not strictly collide. One measures trade volumes, the other the cost of shipping as a share of what is shipped. Levinson himself does not claim to settle it; his book deliberately avoids a quantitative case, because the freight-cost data cannot bear one.
changed: I filed this under logistics for years — a cost-reduction story. It's really a standards story. The decisive act was the corner fitting being released rather than licensed — Tantlinger's design, patented in Sea-Land's name and then given up, because a proprietary container is just a box and a universal one is an economic system.
